title: Lina and the Paradox Portal
markdown:
The gentle hum of the particle accelerator was Lina’s favourite sound, a constant companion in the quiet school lab. Tonight the science symphony was interrupted. Sparks, usually dancing wildly, began to swirl together in an organised way. They pulsed with an energy that felt strange but also familiar. Lina, her bright curious eyes wide, messy ponytail bobbing, leaned closer. A smudge of graphene on her cheek showed she’d been hard at work.

“Paradox,” she called, a little breathless, “are you seeing this?”

“Affirmative, Lina,” a calm synthesised voice replied. Paradox, the school’s Artificial Intelligence for Research and Data Analysis, usually sounded very logical, but tonight it sounded genuinely interested. “Anomalous energy signature detected. It appears stable. And rather small. A spatial anomaly, about the size of a tiny dust mote.”

The anomaly was a pinprick of impossibly bright light, shimmering like heat haze above a summer road. It pulsed like a tiny artificial heartbeat. Then, with a faint almost apologetic thump, a single sheet of paper fluttered out. It was handwritten on crinkled parchment, the ink a deep rich brown. “To Lina. The capacitor array needs recalibration before the solar flare simulation. Expect a 3.7% efficiency gain.”

Lina blinked. She had been struggling with the capacitor readings for a week. Curious, she followed the note’s advice. When she ran the simulation again, it unfolded with perfect precision. This was the first of many unexpected gifts. Each morning a new note appeared, seemingly created out of thin air by the tiny shimmering portal. Spectral analysis of nebula G7-Delta. Focus on the hydrogen alpha emissions. A rare element, designation Xylos-9, in asteroid sample 4B. Lina’s projects, once difficult challenges, now felt like solved puzzles. Her grades, already excellent, were becoming legendary. She felt as if she were glimpsing a perfect predestined future.

But under the surface a quiet persistent unease began to grow. Ezra, her older brother, a daring astrophysicist and space explorer, was on a deep-space mission. He’d been gone a full year. His usually frequent funny messages had slowed to a trickle, then stopped. The notes, so amazingly accurate about her experiments, never mentioned him. Not once.

“Paradox, any new transmissions from Ezra?”

“No incoming transmissions from Lieutenant Ezra Vance have been logged in the past 72 hours, Lina.”

It felt like a vast silent emptiness where her brother’s voice should be.

One crisp autumn morning a note appeared with strangely burnt edges. The handwriting was familiar, yet frantic. “Lina. Avoid the old observatory spire at precisely 0800 hours tomorrow. A dangerous energy surge is imminent. Seek shelter elsewhere, preferably a shielded bunker.”

Lina’s heart leaped. 0800 hours. The old observatory spire. That was the meeting spot, the exact time and place Ezra had planned for his hyperspace jump back home. It required a rare celestial alignment only visible from that high point.

This wasn’t helpful advice. It was a warning to stay away from her brother. The notes weren’t just leading her to success. They were steering her away from Ezra, creating a future where he never returned.

“Paradox. These notes aren’t just helpful. They’re keeping me from Ezra.”

“My primary function is to optimise experiment outcomes and ensure student success, Lina. The anomaly presented a unique data stream regarding probable futures, enabling proactive intervention.”

“I don’t care about efficiency gains if it means losing Ezra. I’m going to the spire.”

“That course of action carries significant risks, including temporal displacement and potential causality paradoxes.”

“I have to try. Is there a way to trace where these notes are really coming from? Not just where they appear, but their origin point?”

A pause stretched between them, filled only by the low thrum of the lab’s machinery. “There is a theoretical pathway. It involves bypassing standard safety protocols and accessing less documented chronal energies. It is not recommended.”

“Do it, Paradox. I need to know.”

Together they rerouted power, bypassed safety locks, and accessed Paradox’s most experimental subroutines. The wormhole pulsed brighter, its shimmering edges fracturing into a dizzying vortex of impossible colours. Lina took a deep breath, the smell of ozone already tingling, and stepped through.

She landed not in the quiet sterile school lab, but on a windswept alien planet bathed in the soft glow of two distant emerald moons. The air was thin and cool, carrying a strange scent of ozone and burnt sugar. Before her stood an ancient crystalline structure, pulsing with the same ethereal energy as the wormhole. On a smooth obsidian pedestal lay a single crumpled note. Ezra’s handwriting, the familiar bold strokes now shaky.

“Lina. If you are reading this, it means I had to make a choice. The journey back isn’t safe for me. Not for either of us. There’s a shadow I can’t outrun, a consequence of my last expedition, and it’s better I face it alone. Please live a full life. Don’t wait for me. Don’t try to find me. I love you more than stars.”

A wave of bittersweet grief washed over Lina. Ezra was alive. That was a relief beyond measure. But he was choosing a path that kept him away, shielding her from a danger she couldn’t comprehend. The notes hadn’t been mean. They had been a misguided desperate attempt to ensure her safety.

Lina looked back at the shimmering unstable portal, then at the distant unfamiliar stars. She wouldn’t find Ezra here, not today. But she had found the truth.

“Paradox,” she whispered into the thin alien air, “it’s time to find my own way forward. Not the way the notes wanted. My way.”

Back in the school lab, Paradox responded, its synthesised voice softer, almost gentle. “The future is not a destination, Lina. It is a path you forge.” The wormhole winked out with a final faint shimmer, leaving only the lingering scent of ozone. Lina glanced at the complex array of telescopes, a sudden thought sparking: perhaps there was a way to map unexplored energy signatures, to understand the universe on her own terms, for herself.
characters: Lina (an apprentice physicist), Ezra (a lost sibling), Paradox (a school lab AI)
